research_text:
# Research brief

## 1. API and meaning of the finding

`javax.crypto.spec.IvParameterSpec` is an `AlgorithmParameterSpec` that carries an initialization vector (IV). Its one-argument constructor copies the supplied byte array; its three-argument constructor copies the selected range. `getIV()` returns a new array. The class does not generate an IV or document a check of its randomness.  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec.html))

The reported message concerns the **`iv` byte-array argument at the `IvParameterSpec(byte[])` constructor event**. The CrySL rule requires the predicate `randomized[iv]`; the message says that the analyzer did not observe a randomized source. The rule does not itself define that message or explain which sources and transformations establish the predicate. The finding alone does not establish the later cipher mode or whether the object is used for encryption or decryption.  
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl))

## 2. Documented usage and remediation guidance

- The `IvParameterSpec` API documentation specifies how to supply and copy IV bytes; it does **not** prescribe a universal remedy for a reported lack of randomized provenance. The appropriate IV properties depend on the cryptographic operation and mode. Oracle’s JCA guide generally says an IV should be random; NIST’s mode-specific guidance distinguishes, for example, unpredictable IVs for CBC and CFB from unique IVs for OFB.  
  Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/20/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html ; https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-38a.pdf ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/20/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))
- Where random bytes are appropriate, Oracle documents `SecureRandom` as a cryptographically strong generator and `nextBytes` as a way to obtain them. Alternatively, a cipher initialized for encryption without required parameters may generate them, but Oracle also allows **provider-specific defaults**; generation must not be assumed to imply random parameters for every provider. Generated parameters can be retrieved through `Cipher.getParameters()` or `getIV()`.  
  Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/SecureRandom.html ; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/SecureRandom.html))
- For **decryption**, Oracle says the same parameters used for encryption must be supplied. Consequently, a previously stored or transmitted IV can be the appropriate input; generating a replacement during decryption is not the documented approach.  
  Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/20/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/20/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html?utm_source=openai))

## 3. Compatibility and migration

Oracle documents retrieving generated parameters, encoding them where needed, and reinstantiating them for decryption. The IV or other required parameters therefore need to remain available to the decrypting party. The cited `IvParameterSpec` documentation does **not** define a persisted or wire format, backward-compatibility scheme, or migration path for changing an existing format.  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html?utm_source=openai))

`IvParameterSpec` is documented as available since Java 1.4 and Android API level 1. Availability of a particular cipher transformation or provider is a separate question. For context, `GCMParameterSpec`, which also carries a GCM authentication-tag length, is documented since Java 1.7 and Android API level 19; that does not by itself establish compatibility with a particular provider or existing format.  
Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec.html ; https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec ; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/GCMParameterSpec.html ; https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/crypto/spec/GCMParameterSpec ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec.html))

## 4. Exact CrySL rule

The supplied source declares `SPEC javax.crypto.spec.IvParameterSpec` and the following matching event clause, verbatim:

```text
EVENTS
	c1: IvParameterSpec(iv);
	c2: IvParameterSpec(iv, offset, len);
	Con := c1 | c2;
```

The declared events are the one- and three-argument `IvParameterSpec` constructor forms. The rule declares `iv` as `byte[]` and `offset` and `len` as `int`, so its event declarations **do constrain the argument lists**. They are not a wildcard for arbitrary methods. **No: as declared, the rule is not a name-only rule matching an unrelated method merely because it shares the name.** The file does not specify the analyzer’s implementation of method resolution, so it cannot independently establish how every analyzer handles an anomalous match. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl))

For `Con`, the rule declares the required predicate `randomized[iv]`; it also declares `length[iv] >= offset + len`, `offset >= 0`, and `len > 0`, and ensures `preparedIV[this]`. These are declarative requirements, not a runtime `if` clause. The file does not explain how the `offset` and `len` constraints are applied to `c1`, which binds only `iv`.  
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl))

**Source limitation:** The rule URL points to the mutable `master` branch. The supplied SHA-256 was not independently computed for the retrieved file, so the retrieved text cannot be confirmed here as the exact hashed version.
